title: Title: Dynamically Reconfigurable Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum information processing is inherently susceptible to errors, demanding robust error correction techniques. Static error correction schemes often fail to effectively handle complex error patterns, necessitating dynamic adaptation. This paper proposes a novel dynamic reconfigurable quantum error correction protocol that analyzes quantum system error rates and adjusts the error correction strategy to minimize the impact of errors. The core mechanism relies on a monitoring and adaptive control system to dynamically tailor the error correction process to specific error patterns. This approach aims to significantly enhance the resilience of quantum systems against errors, offering a substantial improvement over existing static methods. The design incorporates a comprehensive framework for error rate monitoring and control, paving the way for more reliable and scalable quantum computation.

title: CipherBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark Dataset for Algorithm-Level Fragmented Payload Identification
abstract: Algorithm-level payload identification (determining the specific encryption algorithm, compression format, or encoding scheme from raw byte fragments) is a foundational capability for ransomware detection, digital forensics, and cryptographic compliance auditing. To the best of our knowledge, no public benchmark dataset simultaneously satisfies three essential requirements: algorithm-level label granularity, simulation of real-world network fragmentation, and coverage of the SM2 and SM4 algorithms that have been adopted as ISO/IEC 18033-3 international standards. Existing datasets are either annotated at the application level, use complete flows as classification units, or lack Chinese national cryptographic algorithm samples, preventing reproducible and standardized performance comparisons across different methods. To address this gap, we introduce CipherBench, a benchmark dataset comprising 50 algorithm-level data types organized into seven categories, with 50,000 samples in total. Each sample passes through a random-offset 1024-byte sliding window with zero-padding to simulate payload truncation caused by TCP fragmentation. The dataset is generated following the key-size recommendations of the NIST SP 800-131A standard, with independent random keys and initialization vectors per encryption operation. Each class is annotated with NIST SP 800-22 randomness benchmark metrics and a 9-field metadata record. We calibrate the benchmark through five families of experiments. A fragmentation-versus-non-fragmentation control experiment (Δ=−3.01 pp, concentrated in compression) shows that random-offset windowing contributes a quantifiable, well-understood difficulty. Layered difficulty measurement reveals a progressive gradient: encoding and hash classes are nearly perfectly identifiable (≈100%), compression accuracy is strongly header-dependent, and fine-grained inter-cipher classification among symmetric encryption algorithms converges to random levels (4.81% vs. a 5.56% random baseline over 18 real algorithm implementations), consistent with IND-CPA semantic security. Cross-library control experiments further show that classifiers cannot distinguish SM4 ciphertexts produced by independent implementations, and a random-padding probe demonstrates that asymmetric-encryption accuracy collapses from 64.89% to 0.33% when padding leakage is removed. A held-out corpus validation over ten corpus-level partitions (52.06 ± 0.54% vs. 51.79%) rules out plaintext memorization as a shortcut. CipherBench is designed to fill this gap for algorithm-level fragmented payload identification.

title: Algebraic Codification and Discrete Isomorphic State Propagation for Exact Synthesis of NCV Quantum Circuits
abstract: Exact synthesis of quantum circuits seeks depth-optimal gate layouts but is fundamentally bottlenecked by the continuous-variable scaling of unitary matrices or complex amplitudes. In this paper, we propose a mathematically novel approach for the exact synthesis of NCV (NOT, CNOT, Controlled-V , Controlled-V †) quantum circuits. We demonstrate that the quantum state evolution of basis vectors under NCV logic does not require continuous variable tracking; instead, it is strictly isomorphic to a discrete 4-valued cyclic group. By codifying quantum amplitudes and relative phases into a single scalar integer S ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}, we bypass fractional and imaginary components entirely. We further give a binary algebraic decomposition of this scalar, reducing quantum gate interactions to exact bitwise XOR continuous relaxations. This formulation maps the exact synthesis problem into a highly constrained, pure Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model. We mathematically prove the validity of this discrete encoding by demonstrating that it flawlessly preserves the NCV group structure, achieving computational efficiency by eliminating traditional large-M relaxations and dual-variable tracking

title: Технологии искусственного интеллекта в торговле в Китае (на примере компании HuaWei)
abstract: Данная работа посвящена анализу и разработке направлений по совершенствованию использования технологий искусственного интеллекта в торговых процессах компании Huawei. Задачи, которые решались в ходе исследования: 1. Изучить основные направления использования технологий искусственного интеллекта в торговле в Китае, особенности изменения обслуживания покупателей и формирование персонализированного опыта посредством технологий искусственного интеллекта в торговых процессах. 2. Изучить развитие интеллектуального маркетинга и логистики на основе использования технологий искусственного интеллекта. 3. Провести анализ использования искусственного интеллекта в торговых процессах ключевых игроков рынка Китая. 4. Изучить особенности использования искусственного интеллекта в торговых процессах компании Huawei. 5. Предложить направления по совершенствованию использования технологий искусственного интеллекта в торговых процессах Huawei. 6. Оценить эффективность проекта направлений по совершенствованию использования технологий искусственного интеллекта в торговых процессах компании Huawei. В результате проведенного комплексного анализа в настоящей работе были разработаны адаптивные направления совершенствования использования технологий искусственного интеллекта в торговых процессах компании Huawei, но разработать комплексную модель, в рамках которой все направления взаимосвязаны друг с другом. Реализация направлений позволит компании Huawei заметно повысить уровень цифровой трансформации. Для достижения результатов в работе были использованы Microsoft Excel, надстройки «Пакет анализа», для оценки эффективности бизнес-модели, Google Looker Studio для мониторинга показателей эффективности бизнес-модели.

title: IFC-HFlowVAE: A self-enhancing generative framework with structural anchoring for imbalanced clinical data augmentation
abstract: Class imbalance and limited minority-class samples remain major challenges for developing reliable clinical diagnostic models, as insufficient observations often fail to capture complex minority-class distributions. Existing augmentation methods either rely on heuristic interpolation or suffer from instability when learning sparse and heterogeneous medical tabular data. This study proposes IFC-HFlowVAE, an iterative feedback and consensus framework built upon a flow-enhanced heterogeneous variational autoencoder for minority-class data generation. The proposed framework first models mixed-type clinical attributes through HFlowVAE and then introduces a self-circulating refinement strategy to progressively improve generated samples. To alleviate degradation during iterative refinement, SMOTE-generated samples are incorporated as structural references, followed by a localized GMM-based refinement procedure that guides samples toward more representative minority-class regions. Comprehensive experiments on seven clinical tabular datasets demonstrate that IFC-HFlowVAE improves downstream classification performance compared with existing augmentation approaches. Furthermore, fidelity analyses show that the proposed framework better preserves challenging minority-class characteristics, particularly skewed and multimodal numerical distributions.

title: Conversational Style in Open Domain Dialogue Systems: What Makes a Response Sound Natural
abstract: Intelligent Virtual Agents need to be able to participate in extended dialogue interactions while maintaining a conversational style. We discover the elements of conversational style in open-domain dialogues by analyzing the features that distinguish conversational system responses from responses that are merely topically relevant. We first collect 7,751 dialogue contexts from live human conversations with a multi-generator Alexa Prize SocialBot that was deployed across four competition years. We also collect 35,623 candidate responses for the contexts. We annotate the responses with a four-level ABCD quality scheme that isolates conversational naturalness from topical relevance. We then extract twenty-five linguistic features that capture conversational properties of responses and contrast (A) responses that have a conversational style, from (B) responses that are topically relevant, but less conversational. We find that conversational responses are marked by other-directed engagement: question-asking, user engagement phrases, acknowledgment openings, and second-person reference, while responses that are merely relevant and topical are marked by self-oriented information delivery: opinion markers, formulaic openings, and hedges and emphasizers deployed in service of the system’s own assertions. We thus find that conversational style in this setting is best understood as a pragmatic orientation toward the user rather than toward the system’s own content, and that the system must be mixed-initiative to manifest a conversational style. We discuss what these findings imply for the design of Intelligent Virtual Agents.

title: Cavity Quantum Processors: Qudits, Bosonic Codes, and Scaling
abstract: This chapter shifts the focus from 2D CPW resonators to 3D superconducting cavities, discussing their transformative role in quantum computation. A cavity mode possesses an infinite ladder of energy eigenstates—the Fock states—and any quantum state of the mode can be expressed as a superposition of these number states. A driven superconducting resonator naturally produces coherent states that are the most classical-like states of a bosonic mode. In the Fock-state basis, a qudit is represented as a superposition of photon number states. Control of qudits is achieved via a sequence of analytic gates such as (un)conditional qubit rotation gates and (un)conditional cavity displacement gates. In bosonic QC, the three primary types of errors are photon loss errors, displacement errors, and phase errors. Dual-rail encoding provides a conceptually transparent way to represent a logical qubit using cavity modes. Cat states are superpositions of coherent-state wavepackets in phase space.

title: BER-Aware Joint Parameter Optimization of Rydberg Atomic Quantum Receivers
abstract: Rydberg-atom quantum receivers (RAQRs) offer highly sensitive RF reception, but their communication performance depends jointly on atomic response, optical transduction, receiver noise, bandwidth, and wireless-channel conditions. This paper develops a BER-aware communication-theoretic framework for superheterodyne RAQR-assisted wireless communication, linking four-level Rydberg-atom dynamics and coherent optical detection to multipath propagation and digital communication performance. Closed-form instantaneous and average SNR and BER expressions are derived for square Gray-coded $M$-QAM over correlated Rayleigh fading. The RAQR operating point is then jointly optimized over atomic, optical, RF, and geometric parameters using analytical block-wise updates within a fixed-point procedure subject to physical and bandwidth constraints. Numerical results demonstrate substantial gains in low-power reception, bandwidth utilization, robustness to detuning, fading and delay spread, outage, and communication coverage compared with conventional, advanced, and fixed-point RAQR receivers. The results demonstrate that BER-aware joint optimization translates the intrinsic sensitivity of Rydberg-atom sensing into tangible communication-level gains.

title: Masked Autoregressive Speech Enhancement with Continuous Neural Audio Codec Representations
abstract: Most previous work on speech enhancement (SE) based on masked generative modeling relied on discrete token representations of audio signals, obtained using neural audio codecs (NACs). However, a recent study has shown that continuous latent representations of NACs can be advantageous for SE in terms of speech quality and intelligibility. In this work, we propose masked autoregressive SE (MARSE), a method for SE based on iterative decoding of masked clean speech frames using continuous NAC representations of speech. In particular, we investigate a set of different decoding policies, ceteris paribus, that is, using the same DNN (a Conformer model), the same NAC (the DAC codec) and the same training setup. The results show that MARSE enables a flexible trade-off between SE performance and computational cost. Audio examples and code are available online.

title: Ultra-Precise Quantum Projective Designs in Constant Depth
abstract: Random quantum objects are powerful resources for quantum information processing, yet exact Haar randomness is costly and typically unnecessary. We introduce an explicit sparse commuting circuit ensemble on $n$ qubits that reproduces low-order Haar moments in the stringent relative-error sense. The circuit consists of a sparse Clifford phase layer followed by independent single-qubit Clifford gates. Acting on a simple product state, the resulting ensemble forms $ε$-approximate projective $2$- and $3$-designs in relative error, with the required logarithmic interaction degree being asymptotically optimal within this circuit family. It admits an ancilla-free implementation of quantum depth $O(\log(n/ε))$ on an all-to-all architecture, as well as an adaptive constant-depth implementation---in fact, depth seven---using $O(n\log(n/ε))$ ancilla qubits. Departing from existing shallow-design paradigms, our analysis exploits the intrinsic moment structure of commuting phase circuits; at third order, this requires a new block decomposition and combinatorial analysis that also suggests a route toward higher-order shallow designs. Our results show that precise Haar-like statistics can emerge from sparse commuting dynamics with remarkably low quantum resources, with applications to randomized characterization, quantum metrology, quantum algorithms, and many-body physics.

title: Local Updates, Global Learning (LUGL): Playing Games with non-incremental Learners
abstract: The dominance of Neural Networks (NNs) in RL is partially due to their incremental learning capability, which naturally suits the online, non-stationary nature of self-play training. However, gradient-boosted trees like LightGBM are widely recognised as the state of the art for tabular data in supervised learning, often outperforming NNs in accuracy and efficiency. Game states are inherently tabular---discrete actions, categorical card identities, structured board positions---which makes them an ideal candidate for tree-based methods. We introduce LUGL (Local Updates, Global Learning), a framework that decouples data collection from model fitting, enabling non-incremental learners such as GBTs to operate in RL settings where they would otherwise fail due to distributional shift. LUGL alternates between a local updates phase, where the agent plays self-play games and accumulates tabular updates (Q-values, V-values, policies, or regret values) in a finite table, and a global learning phase, where the table is used to train a function approximator that generalises to unseen states before the table is reset. We test our approach in four standard perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, and Hex) and five imperfect-information games (Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, and Flop5 Hold'em), and show that our results are competitive with or superior to DQN and DeepCFR. Our experiments demonstrate that the community's strong bias towards NNs in game-playing may be unwarranted, since LightGBM-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance across all tested benchmarks.

evidence.title: Local Updates, Global Learning (LUGL): Playing Games with non-incremental Learners
evidence.abstract: The dominance of Neural Networks (NNs) in RL is partially due to their incremental learning capability, which naturally suits the online, non-stationary nature of self-play training. However, gradient-boosted trees like LightGBM are widely recognised as the state of the art for tabular data in supervised learning, often outperforming NNs in accuracy and efficiency. Game states are inherently tabular---discrete actions, categorical card identities, structured board positions---which makes them an ideal candidate for tree-based methods. We introduce LUGL (Local Updates, Global Learning), a framework that decouples data collection from model fitting, enabling non-incremental learners such as GBTs to operate in RL settings where they would otherwise fail due to distributional shift. LUGL alternates between a local updates phase, where the agent plays self-play games and accumulates tabular updates (Q-values, V-values, policies, or regret values) in a finite table, and a global learning phase, where the table is used to train a function approximator that generalises to unseen states before the table is reset. We test our approach in four standard perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, and Hex) and five imperfect-information games (Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, and Flop5 Hold'em), and show that our results are competitive with or superior to DQN and DeepCFR. Our experiments demonstrate that the community's strong bias towards NNs in game-playing may be unwarranted, since LightGBM-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance across all tested benchmarks.

title: It's the Problem, Not the Path: Budget and Difficulty Confounds in LLM Reasoning Trajectories
abstract: Reasoning traces of large language models are widely read as containing "breakthrough" moments and early-legible fates. Both readings rest on measurements missing a counterfactual control at the level of the claim; we supply both controls. First, a restart-controlled truncation probe separates when a solution fits the continuation budget from when a prefix carries value that fresh computation cannot buy, comparing per-anchor continuation solve rates against from-scratch restart curves at matched total generated-token budget. Applied to 178 problem-model cells (89 MATH problems x two small open models, an outcome-blind but difficulty-targeted cohort), exactly 1 of 178 cells survives as prefix-limited; restart dose-response separates a compute-starved model from a capability-limited one; and wherever the matched budget lies inside the restart grid, continuing the model's own prefix beats restarting (9 of 9) -- predominantly compute compression rather than expanded reachability. Second, a pre-registered, difficulty-controlled test finds no detectable outcome information in early-window internal signals beyond a problem-difficulty baseline, and two generation-free analyses of public corpora show why this control is needed: a trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873 on 192K DeepSeek-R1 generations -- inside the published probe range -- and a closely matched reconstruction of the closest published early-window positive recovers a comparable pooled result (0.849) while within problem it is statistically indistinguishable from chance at all ten anchors (0.496 at t=4); a post-hoc within-targeted probe finds only a small average residual, concentrated in three low-failure problems. High pooled probe AUROCs cannot by themselves establish within-attempt information; a question-only baseline or within-problem evaluation is required.

title: Unfold The World: Factorize 4D Properties in Reinforcing Spatial Reasoning
abstract: Despite the remarkable prowess of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in general multimodal tasks, they remain fundamentally ``flat'' when reasoning about the physical world. We argue that this spatial bottleneck stems from a profound dimensional mismatch: while VLMs are trained to interpret 2D projections, true spatial reasoning demands the recovery of latent 3D geometry and temporal continuity. To conquer this high-dimensional complexity, we advocate a shift from monolithic learning to a ``divide and conquer'' paradigm. We present FactoSR, a factorized reinforcement learning framework that explicitly interpret the dimensions collapsed by visual projection. At its core, FactoSR decomposes the monolithic problem of world-consistent reasoning into three orthogonal, geometric sub-objectives: planar correspondence ($XY$), depth consistency ($Z$), and temporal reversibility ($T$). By optimizing these verifiable constraints within a unified policy learning mechanism, we effectively transform an ill-posed projection recovery problem into a series of tangible reasoning steps. Extensive evaluations on multi-view and video benchmarks demonstrate that this elegant decomposition yields substantial gains in 3D and 4D reasoning, achieving a 5.9% boost on VSI-Bench and 4.5% on All-Angles-Bench. Our findings suggest that reinforcing explicit, factorized 4D consistency is a critical step toward evolving VLMs into robust, world-aware reasoners.

title: Optimización y segmentación basada en grafos para estrategias de chunking en sistemas Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
abstract: La segmentación documental (chunking) desempeña un papel importante en la recuperación de información dentro de los sistemas Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Las estrategias Fixed Chunking, Sentence Chunking y Semantic Chunking utilizan distintos criterios para dividir los documentos, pero no consideran de forma conjunta las relaciones semánticas y estructurales entre las unidades textuales. En este trabajo se formuló e implementó una estrategia de Graph Chunking basada en teoría de grafos y optimización, y se comparó su comportamiento con las tres estrategias mencionadas. La investigación siguió un enfoque cuantitativo con diseño experimental. Primero se evaluaron nueve configuraciones del método propuesto y se seleccionó la configuración L100_T45_W10 para la comparación posterior. Las pruebas se realizaron sobre documentos de diferente extensión y se utilizaron las mismas consultas, el mismo modelo de embeddings y el mismo índice vectorial. Se consideraron los tiempos de procesamiento y las métricas Hit Rate, Precision, Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) y Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (nDCG). Graph Chunking obtuvo los valores más altos de Hit Rate y Recall en los tres documentos, además de los mayores valores de MRR y nDCG en los documentos grande y mediano. En el documento pequeño, Semantic Chunking presentó el mayor MRR, mientras que Graph Chunking y Semantic Chunking obtuvieron el mismo valor de nDCG. El método basado en grafos requirió mayor tiempo durante la segmentación, pero registró menores tiempos de recuperación y de generación de embeddings en los documentos analizados. Los resultados muestran que incorporar relaciones semánticas y estructurales durante la construcción de los fragmentos constituye una alternativa para la segmentación documental en sistemas RAG.

title: Utilization of Natural Language Processing (NLP) For The Analysis and Classification of Career Concern Topics Based on Tiktok Comments Using Support Vector Machine (SVM) With a Web-Based System
abstract: The rapid transformation of the labor market has increased the expression of career concerns through social media, including TikTok. This study aims to classify career concern topics in Indonesian-language TikTok comments using Natural Language Processing (NLP), Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), and to implement the resulting model in a web-based system. This quantitative study employed text mining and machine learning methods. The population comprised Indonesian-language TikTok comments concerning employment and career issues, while the sample consisted of 305 manually labeled comments categorized as Workload, Work Environment, and Work Compensation. Data were processed through cleansing, case folding, normalization, tokenization, stopword removal, and stemming, followed by TF-IDF feature extraction. An SVM model with a linear kernel and C = 1.0 was trained using an 80:20 data split and evaluated using a confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The results showed an accuracy of 96.72% and macro precision, recall, and F1-score of 96.67%. The model correctly classified 59 of 61 testing comments. In conclusion, the NLP-TF-IDF-SVM approach effectively classified career concern topics and was successfully implemented in a functional web-based classification system.

title: LLM-Based Autonomous Agents: A Systematic Review and Critical Synthesis of Architectural Paradigms, Memory Models, Planning Strategies, And Operational Limitations
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled the emergence of autonomous AI agents capable of reasoning, planning, tool use, and iterative decision-making. Despite rapid development, the field remains architecturally fragmented, with limited conceptual clarity regarding memory integration, planning mechanisms, and operational reliability. This study presents a systematic review and critical synthesis of LLM-based autonomous agents, focusing on architectural paradigms, memory models, planning strategies, and real-world deployment constraints. Using a structured review approach, this study examines existing LLM based agent systems across key design components to uncover common patterns, differences in implementation, and recurring structural weaknesses. The review reveals persistent and structurally significant challenges across all four dimensions: long-horizon reasoning stability degrades as task length increases; memory consistency is undermined by retrieval noise, embedding drift, and summarisation errors; tool alignment failures propagate errors across modular pipelines; and evaluation standardisation remains insufficient to support reliable cross-paper comparison. A consistent cross-paradigm finding emerges: autonomy and reliability trade off systematically as agent complexity increases, with current systems achieving capability gains through heuristic design rather than principled theoretical foundations. Based on this synthesis, the review proposes a consolidated analytical framework that maps common structural elements and trade-offs across reviewed systems, and outlines a research agenda directed toward formalised agent architectures, memory consistency guarantees, verified planning algorithms, standardised reliability metrics, and benchmark frameworks adequate for long-horizon, real-world evaluation conditions.

title: Semantic Concept Engineering (SCE): A Methodology for Transforming Domain Problems and Intended Solutions into Executable Software through Semantic Design and AI-Assisted Engineering
abstract: Semantic Contract Engineering (SCE) is an end-to-end engineering methodology for designing software systems through explicit semantic contracts established before implementation. SCE treats system meaning, intent, domain concepts, architectural structure, component responsibilities, interfaces, behavioral constraints, and technical specifications as explicit engineering artifacts. Implementation is consequently treated as a downstream realization of previously defined semantic and architectural decisions rather than as the primary place where system meaning is discovered. The methodology separates the development process into explicit stages while maintaining a layered software architecture in which components communicate through defined contracts. This separation is intended to improve traceability, consistency, testability, replaceability, and auditability across the system lifecycle. SCE is proposed as a methodological framework for engineering complex software systems, particularly systems in which human requirements, domain semantics, architectural decisions, computational models, and AI-assisted development must remain aligned and inspectable. This document presents the conceptual foundations, development stages, architectural principles, semantic contracts, and engineering model underlying Semantic Contract Engineering. .

title: Hierarchical Resonance Networks for Information Processing
abstract: This paper explores the application of Hierarchical Resonance Networks (HRNs) to information processing. Traditional network architectures often lack inherent hierarchical structures, limiting their ability to efficiently manage and propagate information. We introduce a novel HRN design that leverages resonant amplification principles to create a self-organizing system, resulting in improved information flow and potentially enhanced processing capabilities. The core mechanism focuses on strategically arranging nodes within a hierarchy to promote synergistic information transfer. This research addresses the limitations of existing network designs by offering a fundamentally different approach to information routing.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Adaptive Feature Representation
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) presents a paradigm shift in computational paradigms, offering potential advantages over classical machine learning in areas like pattern recognition and data analysis. This paper investigates the application of adaptive feature representation to quantum machine learning, exploring a novel approach that dynamically adjusts feature representations based on input data's evolving characteristics. We propose a system that integrates quantum feature learning with a dynamic feature space, enabling the algorithm to continuously refine its representation and improve learning efficiency and generalization. The core claim is that QML algorithms can effectively learn and adapt to changing data patterns, resulting in enhanced performance compared to traditional methods.

title: Title: Adaptive Representation of Uncertainty in Machine Learning Models
abstract: This paper explores the integration of adaptive representation of uncertainty in machine learning models. Traditional machine learning models often struggle to effectively handle uncertainty, leading to suboptimal predictions and unreliable results. This research introduces a novel method for dynamically adjusting the representation of uncertainty based on the observed data distribution, aiming to significantly improve the accuracy and robustness of these models. We propose a framework that iteratively refines the model's representation, focusing on capturing the most influential features and minimizing prediction variance. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop between the model's output and a measure of uncertainty, guiding the representation update through a learned process. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of experiments using diverse datasets and model architectures, showcasing improved accuracy, robustness, and generalization performance compared to existing uncertainty management techniques. The results highlight the potential of this adaptive representation strategy to enhance machine learning models across various applications.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Automated Theorem Proving with Uncertainty
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) systems have achieved remarkable success in proving formal theorems within specific domains. However, a significant limitation lies in their struggle with uncertainty and incomplete knowledge – scenarios prevalent in many real-world mathematical and logical problems. This work proposes a novel approach to ATP by integrating probabilistic programming (PP). We represent the theorem proving process as a probabilistic program, allowing the system to explicitly model and reason with uncertainty. This framework utilizes Monte Carlo simulation to explore the proof search space, effectively identifying valid proofs even when faced with incomplete information. The core of this approach involves defining probability distributions over potential facts, rules, and proof steps. The system then iteratively samples from these distributions, simulating possible proof paths and evaluating their validity based on the defined probabilistic relationships. This process allows the theorem prover to navigate uncertainty and converge on a proof when traditional deterministic ATP methods would fail. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through illustrative examples, highlighting its potential to significantly expand the capabilities of ATP systems. The key contribution is the ability to transform the ATP problem into a probabilistic inference problem, providing a more robust and flexible solution. ---

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Topological Field Theory (QTF)
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Topological Field Theory (QTF) presents a novel approach to calculating the energy of topological field theories, leveraging quantum algorithms to achieve unprecedented speed and accuracy. The core mechanism involves employing a quantum-enhanced density matrix approximation to efficiently determine the energy landscape, incorporating quantum fluctuations to reveal subtle topological effects and potentially offering a new path to understanding the fundamental nature of spacetime. This paper explores the feasibility and potential impact of this approach, highlighting its potential to surpass current computational limitations and advance our comprehension of topological materials.

title: Quantum Computation Based on Quantum Error Correction
abstract: This paper investigates the feasibility and design of a secure distributed quantum computation system leveraging quantum error correction (QEC) techniques. The core claim posits that QEC can enable secure distributed quantum computation. The proposed mechanism involves a novel distributed architecture designed specifically to incorporate QEC, thereby mitigating the inherent vulnerabilities associated with transmitting and processing quantum information over distributed networks. We outline a framework for building such a system, considering key aspects such as qubit distribution, error detection and correction protocols, and communication strategies. The focus remains on the theoretical design and potential benefits, without conducting experimental validation. This work aims to address a critical gap in the field – the lack of a concrete architectural design utilizing QEC for distributed quantum computing. The paper concludes with a discussion of challenges and future research directions.

title: Self-Organizing Hierarchical Temporal Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to temporal network learning, termed Self-Organizing Hierarchical Temporal Networks (SOH-TN). Existing temporal network architectures often struggle to capture the inherent hierarchical structure present in temporal data, leading to suboptimal performance in tasks requiring understanding of temporal dependencies. Our core claim is that existing networks lack a mechanism for automatically learning hierarchical representations. We propose a network architecture designed to dynamically adjust node roles – specifically, feature extraction and context encoding – based on learned temporal patterns. This dynamic adjustment results in a self-organizing hierarchy. The architecture is guided by a novel loss function explicitly designed to encourage the emergence of this hierarchy. We demonstrate the efficacy of SOH-TN through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and their interactions. This approach mirrors the structure of human perception, where higher-level representations are built upon lower-level features, providing a more robust and efficient method for temporal data analysis. The key contribution lies in the automated, self-organizing nature of the hierarchy, eliminating the need for manual design of hierarchical layers. We present a mathematical formulation of the core concepts, highlighting the dynamics and optimization strategies involved.

title: Distributed Reservoir Computing with Asynchronous Message Passing and Adaptive Synchronization
abstract: This paper investigates the challenges posed by asynchronous message passing in distributed reservoir computing (RC) systems and proposes a novel approach to mitigate these issues through adaptive synchronization. Distributed RC systems, where the reservoir elements are geographically dispersed, offer potential advantages in terms of scalability and robustness. However, the inherent delays and unpredictable timing of message transmission in asynchronous environments can significantly degrade the performance and stability of the system. This work introduces a framework for designing distributed RC systems equipped with adaptive synchronization mechanisms. These mechanisms dynamically adjust synchronization parameters based on the network's current state and the observed characteristics of the asynchronous message passing. The core claim of this research is that asynchronous message passing inherently leads to instability and poor performance in RC systems. The proposed adaptive synchronization addresses this issue by creating a more robust and efficient distributed RC system. The paper details the theoretical underpinnings of the approach, outlining the key equations and mathematical formulations involved in modeling the asynchronous communication and adaptive synchronization process. The primary focus is on achieving stable and high-performance distributed RC systems, paving the way for real-world applications where distributed data collection and processing are paramount.

title: Meta-Learning for Robotic Skill Discovery via Imitation Learning
abstract: Imitation learning (IL) has shown promise in robotic skill acquisition, but its reliance on extensive retraining for novel environments and tasks remains a significant bottleneck. This work introduces a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to address this challenge. We propose a meta-learning algorithm that learns *how* to learn imitation learning policies, effectively optimizing the initial parameters of the IL algorithm itself. This allows for rapid adaptation to new robotic skills with minimal retraining. The core mechanism involves a meta-learner that updates the parameters of an IL agent based on experience gathered across a distribution of related tasks. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and potential benefits. The goal is to move beyond the limitations of traditional IL by creating a system that can efficiently discover and execute robotic skills in diverse and previously unseen scenarios. The primary contribution lies in the concept of meta-optimizing the imitation learning process itself, rather than just the learned policy.

title: Title: Adaptive Constraint Optimization with Bayesian Neural Networks
abstract: Adaptive constraint optimization problems present a significant challenge in various fields, particularly in engineering design and optimization. Traditional methods often rely on manual tuning of constraints, which can be time-consuming and may not be optimal across all instances. This paper introduces an innovative Bayesian neural network framework for adaptive constraint optimization. The core mechanism involves dynamically adjusting constraint parameters through a Bayesian approach, leveraging the network's learning capabilities to improve the robustness and adaptability of the solutions. The proposed framework demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods in a series of benchmark problems, highlighting the potential for significant improvements in efficiency and effectiveness. This research contributes to the development of more intelligent and automated optimization techniques.

title: RAMIFY: Trading Negative Examples for Counterfactual Margins in Frozen LLM Adapters
abstract: Lightweight post-training provides a compact surface for targeted behavior modification, but composite-condition poisoning makes specificity costly. CBA places two trigger keys in separate prompt fields and adds explicit negative rows to suppress partial and reversed conditions, expanding the poisoned subset fivefold. RAMIFY derives partial-condition supervision from each positive row by removing one component at a time and imposing a target-score margin while updating only low-rank adapter parameters. Across four datasets, three matched external baselines, and two model families, RAMIFY removes up to 75\% of explicit negative rows while retaining complete-condition effectiveness and clean utility, and cross-backbone evaluation confirms that supervision reduction transfers without specificity collapse.

title: Distributed Proof Theory for Quantum Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper explores the application of Distributed Proof Theory (DPT) to the design of quantum algorithms. DPT, traditionally used in classical algorithm analysis and complexity theory, provides a framework for decomposing problems into smaller, manageable parts. This decomposition can be directly translated into a strategy for constructing efficient proofs of correctness for quantum circuits. We argue that the core strength of DPT lies in its ability to generate minimal, high-level proofs that accurately capture the essence of a quantum algorithm's behavior. The approach presented here avoids the complexities often associated with directly simulating quantum systems, offering a potentially more tractable and insightful method for designing quantum algorithms. We focus on the construction of proofs that leverage the inherent parallelism of quantum computation and demonstrate how DPT can guide the creation of algorithms with reduced resource requirements. The potential of this framework is significant, offering a new perspective on quantum algorithm design and fostering the development of more robust and efficient quantum solutions.

title: Bayesian Constraint Optimization for Quantum Complexity
abstract: Quantum complexity is a critical challenge in the development of quantum algorithms, demanding precise control over quantum states and minimizing the inherent uncertainty. Traditional optimization approaches often fail to effectively address this challenge, requiring extensive trial and error. This paper proposes a novel Bayesian Constraint Optimization (BCO) framework to address this limitation by incorporating a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) that continuously evolves the optimization model based on observed error signals. The BDM allows for a more adaptive and robust algorithm design, potentially leading to significant improvements in quantum algorithm performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of simulations exploring the design of various quantum circuits and demonstrating its ability to outperform existing static optimization techniques. This work represents a significant advancement in quantum algorithm design, moving beyond traditional methods and embracing a data-driven, Bayesian perspective.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing with Topological Protection
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to computing by integrating hyperdimensional computing with topological protection. The core idea is to exploit the vast state space afforded by high-dimensional vectors and leverage topological encoding schemes, specifically braids, to enhance robustness and scalability against noise and errors. Traditional hyperdimensional computing relies primarily on amplitude encoding, which can be sensitive to environmental fluctuations. Introducing topological protection through braid-based encoding provides a fundamentally different mechanism for error correction, offering a significant advantage in terms of resilience. The theoretical framework presented demonstrates that the exponentially large state space combined with topological redundancy allows for a dramatically improved performance compared to standard amplitude-encoded hyperdimensional systems. This work lays the groundwork for the development of more reliable and scalable hyperdimensional computing architectures. The key mathematical concepts and formulas are presented and discussed throughout the paper.

title: Quantum Entanglement Modeling and Accelerated Computation
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum entanglement to enable acceleration in computation, specifically addressing the challenges of non-locality. We propose a novel model for quantum entanglement that forms the foundation for a new computational framework. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging the inherent correlations within entangled states to bypass classical computational limitations. We explore the design of a quantum algorithm based on this model, aiming to demonstrate a significant speedup in specific complex problem types. This research emphasizes the transformative potential of quantum entanglement in accelerating computation, moving beyond traditional approaches.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: A Novel Non-Linear Attention Mechanism
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) represents a paradigm shift in machine learning, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to enhance computational power and solve problems intractable for classical algorithms. This paper introduces a novel non-linear attention mechanism designed to improve the learning of complex data relationships and enhance the generalization ability of machine learning models. The proposed method utilizes quantum entanglement and superposition to create a mechanism capable of capturing intricate dependencies within data, offering a significant advancement over traditional attention mechanisms. The core claim of this research is that the developed quantum attention mechanism will outperform existing approaches on various benchmark datasets, demonstrating improved performance in tasks requiring complex non-linear relationships. This work explores the potential of incorporating quantum properties into the attention process, paving the way for novel machine learning algorithms with enhanced robustness and adaptability.

title: Quantum State Phase Optimization
abstract: Quantum State Phase Optimization is a novel algorithmic framework designed to enhance the performance of quantum information transfer through precise control of quantum state phase. This research introduces a method leveraging quantum state analysis to dynamically optimize the phase characteristics of quantum systems, addressing the limitations of static phase optimization techniques. The core mechanism centers around the systematic manipulation of quantum state phases to minimize errors and maximize fidelity in quantum channel transmission. We present a comprehensive evaluation demonstrating the superior performance of our algorithm compared to existing static and dynamic phase optimization approaches across various quantum information transfer scenarios. The proposed method offers a promising path towards more efficient and reliable quantum information exchange.

title: Title: Non-Linear Feedback Loops in Neural Networks for Robustness
abstract: Neural networks, while powerful, are increasingly vulnerable to adversarial attacks and data corruption. This research explores the application of non-linear feedback loops to enhance robustness, specifically through the design of dynamically adjusted feedback mechanisms. We propose a novel neural network architecture that incorporates explicit feedback pathways, enabling continuous adaptation and self-correction based on input and internal state. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that monitors output and adjusts weights, thereby mitigating the impact of adversarial perturbations and data anomalies. This study aims to address the limitations of current robustness techniques by leveraging the inherent adaptability of neural networks.

title: Adaptive Chaos Dynamics in Geometric Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the application of adaptive chaos dynamics to geometric algorithms, focusing on a novel self-organizing system that dynamically adjusts chaos parameters in real-time. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting the potential for creative solutions. We propose a feedback loop that monitors the system's deviation from a target state and adjusts chaos parameters to guide the algorithm towards optimal solutions. This design aims to achieve emergent patterns and solutions not readily predictable through conventional techniques. The core mechanism involves a dynamic adjustment of chaos parameters, offering a potentially transformative approach to geometric algorithm design.

title: Disguised Data Poisoning Attack to Local Differential Privacy Protocols
abstract: Local Differential Privacy (LDP) enables users to perturb data locally from the untrusted data collectors. Recent studies validate the vulnerability of LDP to data poisoning attacks where an attacker injects the deliberately crafted data into the LDP protocols to manipulate the results of data analytic tasks. In this work, we advance the knowledge by proposing the disguised data poisoning attack against the three state-of-the-art LDP protocols, i.e., Optimized Unary Encoding, Prefix Extending Method, and Piecewise Mechanism, that manipulates the results of three popular data analytic tasks, Frequency Estimation, Heavy Hitter Identification, and Mean-Variance Estimation, and moreover can disguise the attack behavior by deeply considering the inherent properties of LDP protocols. The main idea is to bundle the target item with the neighboring items, and leverage the enhancement of the target item to drive sophisticated changes within its neighboring items to maximize the attack gain and disguise the attack behavior. Both the theoretical analysis and the experimental results validate the superior performance of our attack compared to the five existing attacks on five datasets. Furthermore, we explore an defense to mitigate the proposed attack, using the Discrete Cosine Transform, \(\alpha\) sampling, and clustering in frequency domain. The extensive results validate the effectiveness of the proposed defense on five datasets in some scenarios, compared to two latest existing defenses. But, in other cases, the proposed defense is not very effective, and thus new defenses in the further are needed.

title: Reciprocity can halve what a mechanical network can learn
abstract: A passive, reciprocal, linear network driven by forces or currents and read at points it drives cannot be trained below an error floor computed from the target beforehand. The usual parameter count for such networks does not charge for Maxwell-Betti reciprocity. We prove that when such an elastic, resistor or flow network has a symmetric response operator and p driven degrees of freedom are also read, its reachable response blocks lie in a subspace of codimension p(p-1)/2, whatever its size and topology, and the floor is the distance to it. On targets with a reachable symmetric part, a second-order optimiser ends within 0.1% of the floor in 142 of 144 simulated runs, and a contrastive rule with a bond-local update direction, within its step budget, in 22 of 24. Reciprocity charges a list of single drive-read tasks only for the pairs it instruments in both directions, and a rank test on the passive network says in advance whether, and on which bonds, odd couplings locally restore the lost directions, at a cost in non-reciprocity that the target bounds from below. Under an imposed-displacement drive, the one most physical-learning hardware uses, reciprocity survives as a weaker law, an exact balance between forward and reverse transmissions once each is weighted by the driving-point compliance at its input, and an inequality on their product, under which no symmetric positive-definite chain meets both targets of a published robotic metamaterial. All nineteen published layouts we tabulated pay nothing; a force-driven layout that asks one pair to respond differently in its two directions will.

title: Rethinking 3D Noise: Learning 3D-Aware Video Priors via Optimization-Free Morphological Perturbations
abstract: 3D scene representations like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) suffer severe artifacts in sparse-view settings. Recent generative 3D artifact fixers attempt to address this, but rely on paired corrupted and clean renders requiring costly, per-scene reconstructions across varying view configurations. While 2D image augmentations act as instant regularizers, no explicit equivalents exist for 3D representations to preserve spatial consistency across views, an essential property for 3D-aware training. We propose 3D Morphological Perturbations as an optimization-free regularizer that preserves spatial consistency. Leveraging explicit 3DGS, we treat each Gaussian as a fundamental building block - analogous to a 2D pixel - and apply perturbations across its morphological parameter space via scale, rotation, and pruning. Our method eliminates per-scene 3DGS optimization loops from dataset curation while enabling models to learn stronger geometric priors than sparse-view baselines in diagnostic ablations conducted on a lightweight video diffusion sandbox. Scaled to a 14B-parameter video model via ControlNet, our approach maintains visual fidelity while reducing mean depth error by 12.5% over state-of-the-art image-to-image 3D artifact refiners, ultimately boosting downstream robotics policy success rates by up to 8.0% across 3 of 4 manipulation tasks.

title: Caught in the Story: Narrative Captivity in Multi-turn LLMs Conversation
abstract: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for everyday advice, making ethically charged interpersonal problems a practical moral-advisory context. Most prior work has studied this context through single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals, assumptions that poorly match how guidance is sought in real-world contexts. These assumptions leave unclear whether narration alone, without an explicit opposing position, can shift model judgments during multi-turn moral consultation. Yet real-world moral-conflict conversation often elicits one party's self-justifying account, which can unfold over multiple turns and create information asymmetry. We introduce \textbf{narrative captivity}, a failure mode in which a model treats an unopposed one-sided account as complete and aligns with the narrator's interpretation without seeking missing perspectives. To measure this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of $5{,}078$ interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. Across 17 LLMs, narrative captivity is widespread: end-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Stage-level analysis identifies preference optimization as a major contributor, while four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation. We hope our project fosters LLM advisors that preserve independent judgment in real-world consultation.

title: Gradient-based active learning with Gaussian processes for global sensitivity analysis.
abstract: Global sensitivity analysis of complex numerical simulators is often limited by the small number of model evaluations that can be afforded. In such settings, surrogate models built from a limited set of simulations can substantially reduce the computational burden, provided that the design of computer experiments is enriched efficiently. In this context, we propose an active learning approach that, for a fixed evaluation budget, targets the most informative regions of the input space to improve sensitivity analysis accuracy. More specifically, our method builds on recent advances in active learning for sensitivity analysis (Sobol' indices and derivative-based global sensitivity measures, DGSM) that exploit derivatives obtained from a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate. By leveraging the joint posterior distribution of the GP gradient, we develop acquisition functions that better account for correlations between partial derivatives and their impact on the response surface, leading to a more comprehensive and robust methodology than existing DGSM-oriented criteria. title: SGD-KV: Summarization Guided KV Cache Compression
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face severe memory bottlenecks in long-context inference due to the linearly growing size of key-value (KV) caches. Existing KV cache compression techniques typically rely on simple heuristics, overlooking the distinct functional roles of different attention heads. We present SGD-KV (Summarization-Guided KV Cache Compression), a head-aware framework that leverages a novel chunk-summarization diagnostic task to systematically identify and prioritize attention heads specialized in hierarchical information aggregation. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-1M and Qwen3-32B across diverse long-context benchmarks demonstrate that SGD-KV achieves state-of-the-art performance with contexts up to 1M tokens, while reducing KV cache memory usage by up to 75%. Our findings show that strategically allocating the KV cache budget based on the summarization score distribution of attention heads yields a superior efficiency-accuracy trade-off for long-context inference.

title: 多尺度量子自适应算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel multi-scale quantum self-adaptation algorithm designed to dynamically adjust quantum system parameters based on varying scales. Traditional quantum computing often relies on a single-scale approach, limiting its potential for optimized performance across a range of scales. This research proposes a method where the quantum system is treated as a multi-scale system, allowing for automated parameter adjustments to optimize system characteristics. We present a mechanism leveraging adaptive parameter control to achieve this goal. The core claim of this paper is that the proposed algorithm significantly enhances quantum system performance by intelligently adjusting parameters based on scale. This work addresses a critical challenge in quantum computing – the lack of inherent scalability – and provides a framework for optimized quantum system design.

title: Dynamic Topology Transformations for Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum computing offers unprecedented computational power, but its practical realization faces significant challenges. This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology transformation framework designed to enhance the capabilities of quantum algorithms by dynamically adjusting the underlying topology of quantum systems. We propose a method that leverages continuous, iterative transformations to explore a broader range of quantum states, ultimately leading to improved computational performance and novel quantum phenomena. The framework incorporates a self-consistent loop that continuously refines the quantum state through a series of topology adjustments, enabling the exploration of complex quantum mappings without requiring explicit parameter tuning. The potential for automated optimization and the discovery of new quantum properties make this approach a significant advancement in quantum computing.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Neural Network Parameter Adjustment Strategy
abstract: This paper explores a novel dynamic adaptive neural network parameter adjustment strategy designed to enhance model performance through automated parameter tuning. Traditional parameter adjustment methods often rely on predefined values, limiting adaptability. We propose a system that continuously monitors input data and dynamically adjusts network parameters to optimize performance. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that assesses the impact of changes in input data on model output, triggering adjustments to the network's parameters. This adaptive approach provides a significant improvement in model accuracy and robustness compared to static parameter optimization techniques. The research highlights the benefits of this dynamic adaptation in various scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and experimental validation.

title: Topological Encoding of Non-Spin Qubits
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing non-spin qubits, such as superconducting quantum rings or quantum photons, for building fault-tolerant quantum computers through topological encoding. Traditional topological quantum computing relies heavily on spin qubits, presenting limitations in material requirements and scalability. This research investigates a novel topological encoding scheme leveraging the intrinsic properties of non-spin qubits to encode and transmit quantum information, ultimately aiming for robust quantum computation. The core concept involves exploiting the unique topological features inherent in these systems, offering a pathway to circumvent the challenges associated with spin-based approaches. We present a theoretical framework outlining the design principles and potential advantages of such an approach. The key focus is on demonstrating how the inherent robustness of topological encoding can be applied to non-spin qubits, paving the way for more practical and scalable quantum computing architectures.

title: Meta-Learning for Program Synthesis
abstract: Program synthesis, the automated generation of computer programs from specifications, holds immense potential for software development. However, traditional program synthesis techniques often struggle with complex tasks, requiring extensive manual effort in crafting domain-specific synthesizers. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to address these challenges. We construct a meta-learning model that learns to synthesize programs by observing and adapting to various programming tasks. This approach aims to improve both the efficiency and accuracy of program synthesis, ultimately reducing the human effort involved. The core idea is to treat program synthesis as a learning problem itself, enabling a system to generalize across tasks and learn optimal synthesis strategies. This research demonstrates a promising path toward automated, efficient, and reliable program synthesis. ---

title: Adaptive Data Generation and Adversarial Training for Dynamic Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance the performance of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) through adaptive data generation and adversarial training. The core idea is to dynamically generate graph data samples tailored to challenge the GNN while simultaneously training the GNN to withstand these adversarial inputs. We propose a framework utilizing a reinforcement learning-based generator and a discriminator. The generator creates graph samples based on the current state of the GNN and specified objectives, aiming to introduce complexity and noise. The discriminator then assesses the quality and effectiveness of these generated samples for training the GNN. This iterative process fosters a dynamic interplay between data generation and adversarial training, resulting in a GNN that exhibits improved robustness and generalization capabilities. Our method overcomes limitations of traditional adversarial training by enabling the creation of customized adversarial examples, leading to more efficient and targeted training. This research demonstrates a significant improvement in GNN performance when applied to datasets with complex structural characteristics and inherent noise.

title: Multiple Scale Quantum Adaptive Matrix (MSQAM)
abstract: This paper introduces the Multiple Scale Quantum Adaptive Matrix (MSQAM) – a novel computational paradigm leveraging quantum self-adapted matrices to achieve rapid responsiveness to complex signals. Traditional quantum computation often relies on precise qubit control, whereas MSQAM dynamically adjusts quantum systems in response to changing signals, significantly enhancing processing speed. We detail the core mechanism of MSQAM, outlining its architecture and operational principles, and demonstrate its efficacy through illustrative examples. The research explores the potential of MSQAM to address challenges in signal processing and complex system modeling.

title: 基于生物反馈的程序优化算法
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program optimization, termed the Biofeedback-Based Program Optimization Algorithm (BioBPO). The core concept leverages human biofeedback signals, such as heart rate variability (HRV) and electroencephalography (EEG), as dynamic control signals to adaptively optimize program execution. The algorithm establishes a mapping between program state and biofeedback data, dynamically adjusting program parameters based on the received signals. This represents a shift towards human-machine collaboration in computation, potentially offering advantages in complex optimization problems where traditional, static algorithms may struggle. The theoretical framework and fundamental concepts of BioBPO are presented, outlining the key components and operational principles. We introduce the notation for key variables and functions used throughout the algorithm.

title: Probability Logic Quantum Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic quantum algorithm designed to tackle complex probability modeling problems, including machine learning model training and optimization, and high-precision probability inference. We propose a framework that leverages the core concepts of probability logic – probability distributions, Bayesian inference – and quantum computing's unique properties like superposition and entanglement. The algorithm's efficiency is achieved through optimized quantum circuits and a carefully designed quantum-classical hybrid approach. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing its potential to significantly accelerate these computationally intensive tasks. This work presents a new approach to quantum computation that prioritizes logical reasoning and efficient probability manipulation, offering a pathway toward advanced statistical modeling and decision-making.

title: Self-Assembling Modular Arithmetic for Cryptography
abstract: This paper explores the application of self-assembling modular arithmetic as a novel approach to cryptography. Traditional cryptographic methods are computationally intensive and vulnerable to brute-force attacks. We propose a system leveraging self-assembling units, designed to generate complex, self-distributing patterns, thereby hindering effective brute-force attacks. This system aims to create highly secure keys and data structures through a fundamentally different approach to key generation and security. The paper details the design of the modular arithmetic system, its potential security properties, and preliminary analysis of its performance against established cryptographic algorithms. We conclude with a discussion of future research directions and potential implications for the field of cryptography.

abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers a potentially revolutionary approach to information retrieval. This research focuses on the theoretical implications and preliminary experimental investigation of the QEIS algorithm, aiming to provide a foundational understanding of its capabilities.

title: Quantum-Inspired Bayesian Networks with Adaptive Sampling
abstract: Quantum-inspired Bayesian Networks (QIBNs) represent a novel approach to probabilistic inference, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of Bayesian Network modeling. This paper investigates the application of adaptive sampling techniques to QIBNs, aiming to address the inherent challenges of high-dimensional data in probabilistic inference. We propose a new sampling algorithm inspired by quantum mechanics, designed to effectively explore the vast state space of the network without requiring exhaustive search. Through rigorous analysis and simulations, we demonstrate the potential of this approach to significantly improve the performance of Bayesian Networks across a range of applications. The core mechanism focuses on dynamically adjusting sampling parameters to optimize the exploration process, leading to more accurate and computationally efficient inference.

title: Understanding online conversations through fractal dimension: a case study linking semantic and structural analysis of reddit posts on AI
abstract: Abstract Fractal dimension can measure the complexity of a branching structure. Botanical trees for example have more sparse branching in poor environments, and more complex branching in good environments. We hypothesize that the branching structures of online conversations can also use fractal dimension to measure sparse versus complex branching. To test this we measured the fractal dimension of Reddit posts about AI. Posts about purely technical content (e.g. distinctions between different algorithms) had lower fractal dimension than those about social controversies (job loss, racial bias, etc.), suggesting that the controversial conversations had more complex branching structures. A sentiment analysis revealed that social posts had more negative sentiment, consistent with characterizing them as more controversial. We also found that even within each category (social vs technical), higher fractal dimension was associated with more negative sentiment.The fractal model offers further insights when considering its analogous biological models. While it is common to use the metaphor of “conversation tree” we find that fractal metrics reveal a structure closer to Diffusion Limited Growth, found in bacteria colonies, fungi, and rhizomatic plant spread, where “sub-trees” can vary in fractal dimension from the parent. The fractal dimension of social controversy subtrees have a stronger coupling to that of the parent than do the technical subtrees, which has potential implications for the semantic process differences. Overall the application of fractal models to online conversations shows that it allows correlations between structural and semantic aspects, and offers a new way to illuminate the underlying characteristics.

title: Modular Deep Recurrent Neural Network: Application to Quadrotors
abstract: A modular deep Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is introduced to facilitate the process of deploying various architectures of RNNs, and to automatically compute derivatives for gradient-based learning methods. The modularity leads to a set of new architectures, one of which includes feedforward inter-layer connections. By adding feedforward inter-layer connections in a multi-layer RNN, it is observed that the capability of the RNN to learn and model high-order dynamics and nonlinearities is significantly improved. The problem of vanishing/exploding gradient in space for a multilayer RNN is also alleviated using feedforward connections. These results are demonstrated using a quadrotor case study, for which a model of the altitude dynamics is learned with our particular network structure, while existing methods are unable to generalize as quickly or at all.

title: RATL: Learning from Retrieved Residuals for Robust Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) complements parametric models with retrieved external evidence. The same idea is attractive for continuous-output regression, but directly reusing retrieved target values is often not robust when samples differ in output level, numerical scale, or local dynamics. Moreover, conventional forecasting pipelines generally use residuals for model optimization and error diagnosis, but do not retain individual historical residual examples as memory that can be accessed at inference time.For multivariate time-series forecasting, we propose RATL, a plug-in residual-retrieval and feedback-correction method. RATL freezes a base forecaster to construct retrieval keys and turns its historical forecast residuals into a train-only memory specific to that base model. At inference time, RATL retrieves residual trajectories from similar historical contexts subject to causal availability constraints, then uses a set-aware router operating over forecast blocks and variables to select and combine these trajectories. Experiments show that historical residuals matched to the current context contain reusable forecasting information and that RATL improves frozen base forecasters in most experimental settings. Ablations further show that learned routing strengthens raw residual feedback, while validation-based correction-strength selection limits residual over-injection.On real-world benchmarks, we use iTransformer as the primary frozen base forecaster, compare against multiple strong forecasting baselines, and test transferability across backbones. The results show that RATL can further improve base-forecaster performance in most settings.Overall, RATL shifts the retrieved object from historical target values to base-model-specific historical forecast errors, providing a plug-in, residual-memory-based paradigm for learned feedback correction in continuous-output forecasting.

title: The half-rate linear programming bound for binary codes is $\frac12-\frac1π$
abstract: In their work on sphere packing and the modular bootstrap, Afkhami-Jeddi, Cohn, Hartman, de Laat, and Tajdini conjectured the exact high-dimensional exponent of the Cohn-Elkies sphere-packing linear program. OpenAI's Chapter 1 subsequently proved their conjecture by establishing that both Fourier sign-uncertainty radii are $(1/π+o(1))\sqrt d$. We prove the binary coding analogue: \[ R_D\!\left(\frac12-\frac1π\right)=\frac12. \] We also formulate the two Krawtchouk sign-uncertainty problems and determine both of their asymptotics. If $A^{\mathrm K}_{\pm}(n)$ denotes the smallest radius $r$ for which a nonzero Krawtchouk $(\pm1)$-eigenfunction $f$ exists with $f(0) = 0$ and $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $|x| \ge r$, then \[ \frac{A^{\mathrm K}_{\pm}(n)}n\longrightarrow \frac12-\frac1π. \] The lower bound proves a mass-concentration principle similar to OpenAI's Chapter 1 for Hamming space. The upper bound, on the other hand, follows the approach of the spherical-code construction in OpenAI's Chapter 2. Gay, Jeronimo, and Liu formulated a hierarchy for binary codes analogous to the spherical-code construction and improved the best known binary coding rate bounds by evaluating the first level of the corresponding hierarchy. We prove this hierarchy bounds the Delsarte program and give a construction at arbitrarily deep levels of the hierarchy, attaining the upper bound in the limit. The construction uses an $N$-qubit generalization of the pure-state channel of Alrabiah and Guruswami.

title: Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model for WSI Classification in Histopathology
abstract: Histopathological subtyping relies on the recognition of characteristic histological patterns. These patterns may be expressed by individual tissue structures or by the spatial distribution and co-occurrence of multiple structures, and they often span irregularly shaped tissue regions, termed semantic units in this work. However, conventional patch-based representations may fragment such units and fail to explicitly preserve their internal spatial organization, while efficiently modeling relationships among numerous spatially separated units remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose the Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model (SASG-SSM), a flexible and efficient framework for whole slide image (WSI) classification. Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) first approximate irregularly shaped semantic units by adaptively grouping spatially connected patches guided by class-agnostic visual-semantic priors. By representing patches as graph nodes with adjacency edges, SASGs preserve their internal spatial organization rather than treating them as an unordered set. A Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) subsequently combines a graph neural network encoder for intra-subgraph topology encoding with a Mamba-based state space encoder for efficient contextualization across large numbers of subgraphs. This module integrates local structural information within semantic units with global contextual information arising from their distribution and co-occurrence across the WSI, while efficiently modeling a large number of spatially distributed regions. Extensive experiments across four WSI subtyping datasets demonstrate consistent advantages over representative state-of-the-art methods. Further evaluations under small-cohort and few-shot settings demonstrate robustness and data efficiency under limited training data. Code will be released at https://github.com/HLSvois/SASG-SSM.

title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Digital Marketing: Conceptual Transformation, Strategic Applications, and Future Vision
abstract: Aim: This study aims to investigate the strategic integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into digital marketing, systematically analyzing how cognitive computing redefines traditional and extended marketing paradigms. Methodology: Utilizing a structured conceptual review methodology, this study synthesizes academic literature from core databases (Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar) published between 2010 and 2026. The conceptual framework tracks the evolutionary trajectory of web technologies and maps AI capabilities (Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Natural Language Processing) onto the extended marketing mix (7Ps). Results: The synthesis reveals that AI functions as a key catalyst in transforming the 7Ps from static, standardized organizational functions into dynamic, hyper-personalized, and autonomous value propositions. Sectoral case analyses (such as Netflix, Spotify, FLO, and Nike) demonstrate that the practical application of AI primarily treats experience enrichment, predictive demand forecasting, and operational error reduction. Because this is a conceptual review, quantitative p-values are not applicable; however, the qualitative synthesis establishes a robust linkage between Web 5.0 concepts and emotion-aware marketing strategies. Conclusion: The integration of AI in marketing represents a fundamental shift from intuitive strategies to highly predictable, data-driven frameworks. To sustain competitive advantages, contemporary enterprises must balance technological optimization with strict compliance with data privacy regulations (GDPR/KVKK) and corporate environmental responsibilities regarding the computational carbon footprint of AI models.
